domain.name: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization

learning_design.unlock_rule: A knowledge node unlocks after all required prompts are completed, including required table or code discoveries.
learning_design.mastery_note: Exploration progress is not mastery evidence; quiz attempts remain the scored retrieval signal.

prompts.label: WHY MULTIPLE SIGNALS?
prompts.placeholder: Different operational questions need different evidence. What is the core distinction?

reveal.text: Metrics summarize numeric behavior over time, logs preserve detailed records, events describe something that happened, and audit history records API/account activity.

prompts.label: COMPARE THE SIGNALS
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one signal at a time and decide which operational question it answers best.

cells.question: Is CPU, latency, or error rate changing?
Why did this request or process fail?
What happened that should trigger automation?
Who called this AWS API, and when?

prompts.label: READ A METRIC
prompts.placeholder: How do the main pieces of a CloudWatch metric fit together?

prompts.label: DIMENSION OR METRIC?
prompts.placeholder: Reveal each field and connect identity to measurement.

cells.role: Which resource or slice the measurement belongs to
How data points are grouped for evaluation
How values in a period are summarized

prompts.label: WHY USE THE AGENT?
prompts.placeholder: What can the CloudWatch agent provide that standard EC2 metrics may not?

reveal.text: The CloudWatch agent can collect guest operating-system metrics and logs, such as memory usage and local log files, then publish them to CloudWatch.

prompts.label: INSPECT THE AGENT CONFIG
prompts.placeholder: Click the important fields to see what this agent configuration collects and where it sends data.

annotations.title: Guest OS memory metric
annotations.explanation: The agent can publish memory utilization from inside the operating system.

annotations.title: Local log source
annotations.explanation: file_path selects the local file that the agent reads.

annotations.title: CloudWatch Logs destination
annotations.explanation: log_group_name selects the destination log group.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES CLOUDTRAIL ANSWER?
prompts.placeholder: A resource changed. Which question is CloudTrail designed to answer?

reveal.text: CloudTrail records AWS API and account activity so you can investigate which principal made a call, what API was invoked, when it happened, and related request context.

prompts.label: CLOUDTRAIL OR CLOUDWATCH?
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one use case at a time.

cells.need: Who deleted or modified a resource?
Why did an application request fail?

prompts.label: HOW AN ALARM DECIDES
prompts.placeholder: What does a CloudWatch alarm evaluate?

reveal.text: An alarm evaluates metric data against a configured condition across evaluation periods, then changes state based on the result and the configured treatment of missing data.

prompts.label: READ THE ALARM STATES
prompts.placeholder: Reveal each state and connect it to its operational meaning.

cells.meaning: The evaluated condition is not breaching.
cells.operator: No alarm condition is currently active.

cells.meaning: The condition is breaching according to the configured evaluation logic.
cells.operator: Configured alarm actions can run on the state transition.

cells.meaning: There is not enough usable data to determine OK or ALARM.
cells.operator: Check missing-data treatment and whether the metric is still publishing.

prompts.label: FROM LOG TO ALARM
prompts.placeholder: How does a log pattern become an alarmable signal?

prompts.label: WHEN TO USE A METRIC FILTER
prompts.placeholder: A log line contains ERROR but no metric exists. What should you build?

reveal.text: Use a CloudWatch Logs metric filter to turn matching log events into metric data, then graph or alarm on the resulting metric.

prompts.label: WHAT ROLE DOES SNS PLAY?
prompts.placeholder: Why does SNS appear in alarm-remediation designs?

reveal.text: SNS provides pub/sub delivery to supported subscribers and integrations. A CloudWatch alarm can publish a notification to a topic, decoupling alarm detection from downstream recipients.

prompts.label: PICK A NOTIFICATION PATH
prompts.placeholder: Reveal each destination pattern.

cells.need: Send one event to multiple consumers

prompts.label: EVENTBRIDGE MENTAL MODEL
prompts.placeholder: What are the three pieces to think about?

reveal.text: An EventBridge rule matches an event pattern, then routes matching events to one or more targets. The event pattern should be as specific as the use case requires.

prompts.label: INSPECT AN EVENT PATTERN
prompts.placeholder: Click each field to see how the rule narrows EC2 events.

annotations.title: Event source
annotations.explanation: source limits the rule to events emitted by the specified AWS service.

annotations.title: Event type
annotations.explanation: detail-type identifies the kind of EC2 event the rule should consider.

annotations.title: Detail filter
annotations.explanation: The nested detail field filters for the stopped state.

prompts.label: WHAT IS AUTOMATION?
prompts.placeholder: When is Systems Manager Automation a better fit than one ad-hoc command?

reveal.text: Automation runbooks define repeatable multi-step operational workflows with parameters, actions, branching, approvals, and AWS API integrations.

prompts.label: INSPECT A RUNBOOK
prompts.placeholder: Click the control fields to see how this runbook performs a repeatable remediation.

reveal.code:
description: Restart an EC2 instance
schemaVersion: '0.3'
parameters:
  InstanceId:
    type: String
mainSteps:
  - name: restartInstance
    action: aws:executeAwsApi
    inputs:
      Service: ec2
      Api: RebootInstances
      InstanceIds:
        - '{{ InstanceId }}'

annotations.title: Automation schema
annotations.explanation: The schema version tells Systems Manager how to interpret the Automation document.

annotations.title: Automation action
annotations.explanation: aws:executeAwsApi lets a runbook call an AWS API operation.

annotations.title: API operation
annotations.explanation: This step calls the EC2 RebootInstances API using the supplied instance ID.

prompts.label: RUN COMMAND OR AUTOMATION?
prompts.placeholder: Compare the operational scope.

columns.title: Automation
items: Can call AWS APIs and coordinate remediation

prompts.label: WHEN RUN COMMAND FITS
prompts.placeholder: You need to execute a script across a fleet without SSH. What fits?

reveal.text: Run Command can execute commands on managed nodes through Systems Manager without requiring direct interactive shell access.

prompts.label: WHEN LAMBDA FITS
prompts.placeholder: What kind of remediation is a good Lambda target?

reveal.text: Lambda fits short, event-driven remediation that needs custom code or API orchestration, especially when EventBridge or an alarm can provide the trigger.

prompts.label: ADD OPERATIONAL GUARDRAILS
prompts.placeholder: What should a safe remediation function consider?

items: Scope controls so the function changes only intended resources

prompts.label: MATCH THE RELIABILITY FEATURE
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one failure/recovery need at a time.

cells.purpose: Try delivery again according to the configured retry behavior.
Preserve failed deliveries for investigation or later processing.
Store events and replay them later through the event bus.

prompts.label: WHAT DOES COMPUTE OPTIMIZER DO?
prompts.placeholder: Is it a monitoring system or a recommendation system?

reveal.text: Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization and configuration data to generate resource-sizing and optimization recommendations. Treat the recommendation as decision support, then evaluate workload requirements before changing production resources.

prompts.label: READ A RECOMMENDATION
prompts.placeholder: Reveal the evidence you should consider before acting.

cells.why: Shows whether the resource is consistently under- or over-utilized.
Helps judge whether a smaller or different configuration could harm the workload.
Shows the optimization opportunity, not an automatic approval to resize.

prompts.label: TRIAGE THE BOTTLENECK
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one symptom at a time and map it to the next evidence source.

cells.reason: Determine whether compute is saturated or a process is misbehaving.
Separate instance limits from path/security problems.
Identify whether IOPS/throughput/latency is the constraint.

prompts.label: COMPARE PLACEMENT GROUPS
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one strategy at a time and focus on the performance/failure trade-off.

cells.fit: Very low latency / high east-west throughput
cells.tradeoff: Concentrates instances into a smaller failure domain.

cells.layout: Keep a small number of instances on distinct hardware
cells.fit: Critical instances that should be isolated

cells.tradeoff: Application should tolerate a whole partition failing.

prompts.label: CHOOSE BY FAILURE MODEL
prompts.placeholder: What should drive the choice?

reveal.text: Choose the placement strategy from the workload's communication pattern and failure-isolation requirements, not simply from a desire for 'better performance.'

prompts.label: MATCH THE EBS VOLUME
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one EBS family at a time.

cells.key: Baseline performance can be configured independently of volume size within service limits.

cells.fit: I/O-intensive workloads needing provisioned IOPS and high durability
cells.key: Use for sustained, predictable IOPS requirements.
Optimized for throughput rather than small random I/O.
Choose when cost matters more than frequent high performance.

prompts.label: DON'T TUNE BLINDLY
prompts.placeholder: Which signals should you inspect before changing the volume?

reveal.text: Inspect workload latency, queueing, IOPS, throughput, burst/balance behavior where applicable, and the actual access pattern before changing the EBS type or performance settings.

prompts.label: MATCH THE S3 PATTERN
prompts.placeholder: Reveal each performance technique.

cells.idea: Uploads parts independently and supports parallelism/retry of individual parts.
Increases aggregate request throughput when the workload can issue concurrent operations.
Uses the AWS edge network to improve transfer paths for suitable workloads.

prompts.label: CHOOSE THE SHARED STORAGE
prompts.placeholder: Reveal one storage model at a time.

cells.fit: Linux workloads needing shared POSIX-style file access.

cells.interface: Managed file systems for specific engines/protocols
cells.fit: Workloads needing Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS capabilities.
Durable object storage, data lakes, static content, and object-based workflows.

prompts.label: CHOOSE THE RDS SIGNAL
prompts.placeholder: Reveal each monitoring source and learn what layer it helps you investigate.

cells.shows: Service and instance metrics such as CPU, connections, storage, and latency
cells.use: You need time-series health and alarmable metrics.

cells.shows: Operating-system-level process and resource detail from the DB host
cells.use: You need deeper host-level visibility than standard metrics.

cells.shows: Database load and contributors such as waits and SQL
cells.use: You need to investigate database workload bottlenecks rather than only host utilization.

prompts.label: CORRELATE BEFORE CHANGING
prompts.placeholder: What is the safer troubleshooting habit?

reveal.text: Correlate database load, host/resource metrics, connection behavior, and application symptoms before deciding that the database instance simply needs to be larger.

prompts.label: WHAT PROBLEM DOES RDS PROXY HELP WITH?
prompts.placeholder: Think about connection behavior rather than query tuning.

reveal.text: RDS Proxy pools and manages database connections so applications—especially bursty or highly concurrent ones—can reduce connection overhead and handle failover more gracefully.

prompts.label: PROXY OR BIGGER DATABASE?
prompts.placeholder: Separate connection pressure from database compute pressure.

columns.title: RDS Proxy
items: Does not make inefficient SQL inherently faster

columns.title: Scale/tune database
items: Addresses compute, memory, storage, or query bottlenecks
May be needed when the database itself is saturated
Should be guided by monitoring evidence
